title: Is legal reasoning just politics in disguise?
subtitle: Critical legal studies and feminist legal theory
objectives: State the CLS indeterminacy thesis and explain Kennedy's individualism/altruism contradiction in private law doctrine
Distinguish liberal, radical and difference feminist legal theory, and state MacKinnon's dominance critique of law's claimed objectivity
Apply CLS and feminist critiques to a doctrine or fact pattern, and state the strongest scholarly objections to each school

leadingAuthorities.citation: Kennedy, "Form and Substance in Private Law Adjudication" (1976)
leadingAuthorities.role: Foundational CLS text: argues private law doctrine oscillates between irreconcilable individualist and altruist value commitments, so legal reasoning alone cannot compel one outcome
Manifesto-style statement of CLS's aims: exposing the contradictions in liberal legal thought and law's role in legitimating an unchosen distribution of power

leadingAuthorities.citation: MacKinnon, Toward a Feminist Theory of the State (1989)
leadingAuthorities.role: Develops the dominance approach: law's claimed objectivity and neutrality reproduce a male point of view, most visible in law's historical treatment of sexuality and violence against women

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: This is the most self-consciously political material in the module — not because it tells you what to believe, but because it asks you to hold a claim (law is indeterminate; law encodes power) and its best objections in your head at the same time. Where the profile shows knowledge ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You can define indeterminacy — this lesson checks whether you can show it working on a fact pattern, and show where critics think it breaks down.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans on scenarios: you'll be asked to spot indeterminacy or a dominance argument at work, not just define the terms.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and take it slowly — the indeterminacy thesis and the liberal/radical/difference split are the vocabulary the rest of the lesson assumes you already have.

overview.hook: Two judges read the same contract clause, apply the same doctrine, and reach opposite results — and both write judgments that sound perfectly compelled by the law. Critical legal scholars argue this isn't occasional bad luck: it's what legal reasoning is like most of the way down, most of the time it matters. Feminist legal scholars ask a related but different question — not only whether doctrine is indeterminate, but whose experience the 'reasonable person' was built to see as ordinary in the first place. Neither claim is obviously right, and neither is obviously wrong. This lesson asks you to state each with the force its proponents intended, and then to hold the line against it that their sharpest critics — including critics inside the same intellectual traditions — actually make.
overview.lawStatedNotice: This lesson presents contested academic theory rather than settled law. The scholarship is decades old and stable; the debates it describes remain genuinely live in legal academia.

parts.heading: Doctrine that decides itself, or judges who decide doctrine?
parts.voice: argumentative — states the indeterminacy thesis in its strongest form before testing it
body: Ask a first-year law student what a judge does with a hard case, and the usual answer is: applies the relevant rule to the facts. Critical legal studies (CLS), a movement that coalesced in American law schools from the mid-1970s, argues that this picture is close to backwards for a large and important class of cases. Its central claim — the indeterminacy thesis — is that the accepted materials of legal reasoning (statutes, precedents, canons of interpretation, principles) do not, by themselves, compel one correct outcome in contested cases. Something else supplies the missing premise, and that something is political and moral choice, dressed afterwards in the language of deduction.

Duncan Kennedy's 'Form and Substance in Private Law Adjudication' (1976) makes this argument through the unglamorous terrain of contract and tort doctrine rather than constitutional grand cases, which is what gives it its force. Kennedy shows that private law is built from paired opposites at every level: rules versus standards as forms of regulation, and — underneath that — individualism versus altruism as background value commitments. A 'rule' (e.g. a fixed age of majority) trades certainty for occasional harshness in individual cases; a 'standard' (e.g. 'reasonableness') trades certainty for sensitivity to context. Neither form is neutral between the values it tends to serve.

The upshot is not that judges are lying, or that law is 'just politics' in a crude, conspiratorial sense. It is that legal materials genuinely run out before a determinate answer appears, and judges then reach for background commitments — about self-reliance versus mutual responsibility, about which party should bear a risk — that the doctrine itself cannot supply. The judgment that results will still cite authority, still look syllogistic, and still be sincerely written. That is precisely what CLS finds significant: indeterminacy is compatible with, and hidden by, perfectly competent legal craft.

components.definition: The CLS claim that the accepted sources and methods of legal reasoning — statute, precedent, interpretive canons — do not by themselves compel one determinate outcome in a significant range of contested cases; a further, non-legal choice (typically political or moral) is needed to reach a result.

interaction.prompt: Does the CLS indeterminacy thesis claim that judges give no reasons for their decisions, or that the accepted materials of legal reasoning fail to compel one determinate outcome even where reasons are given?
options: That the accepted materials of legal reasoning fail to compel one determinate outcome, even where reasons are given
That judges give no reasons for their decisions at all
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. CLS scholars do not deny that judgments are reasoned and internally coherent — the claim is that the reasoning could, with equal formal competence, have run the other way.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again — CLS scholars accept that judges write careful, reasoned judgments. The claim is narrower and stranger: that the reasoning given does not, on its own, compel the result reached over its opposite.

parts.heading: Unger and the reproduction of power
parts.voice: manifesto — reads Unger's programmatic claims closely
body: Roberto Unger's 'The Critical Legal Studies Movement' (1983) generalises Kennedy's private-law argument into something closer to a manifesto. Unger's target is what he calls liberal legal thought as a whole, and he attacks it on several fronts at once: its formalism (the idea that legal reasoning is a distinct, quasi-mechanical method separable from open moral and political argument); its objectivism (the idea that existing legal doctrine expresses a coherent, defensible scheme of principle rather than a compromise between incompatible interests); and its claim to neutrality between contested visions of social life.

For Unger, law does more than fail to be neutral by accident — it does active work. Doctrine takes a particular, historically contingent settlement of social conflict (over labour, property, the family) and re-describes it as the natural, principled working-out of impersonal legal categories. That re-description is what legitimates the settlement: it makes an outcome that could have gone otherwise look as though it had to come out this way. CLS scholars sometimes called the critical technique for exposing this 'trashing' — taking a body of doctrine that presents itself as coherent and showing, from the inside, that it is actually organised around unresolved and irreconcilable premises.

Unger's own constructive programme — what he called 'expanded doctrinal analysis' and, later, more experimental proposals for institutional reconstruction — is more ambitious and more contested than the critical diagnosis itself, and it is the diagnosis that has had the more lasting influence on legal scholarship. What CLS leaves behind, whatever you think of its remedies, is a standing challenge: show that a given area of doctrine really is coherent, rather than assuming it, the next time it is invoked as simply 'the law'.

components.label: Unger's critique of liberal legal thought
points: Formalism — the claim that legal reasoning is a distinct, quasi-mechanical method, separable from open political and moral argument
Objectivism — the claim that existing doctrine expresses a coherent scheme of principle, rather than an unresolved compromise between conflicting interests

Legitimation — doctrine re-describes a contingent settlement of social conflict as the necessary, principled working-out of neutral legal categories, making it harder to see as a choice that could have gone otherwise
'Trashing' — the critical technique of showing, from within a body of doctrine that presents itself as coherent, that it is organised around unresolved and irreconcilable premises

interaction.prompt: Put these steps in the order a CLS 'trashing' argument typically proceeds.
items: Identify a body of doctrine presented as coherent and principled
Show the doctrine actually rests on two incompatible background values (e.g. individualism and altruism)
Show that outcomes could be justified either way using the same accepted materials
Conclude that the doctrine's apparent coherence is a legitimating appearance rather than a genuine constraint on outcomes
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the shape of the argument: start from doctrine's self-presentation as coherent, locate the buried contradiction, show it can cut either way, and conclude that 'the law made me do it' understates how much work the judge's own choice is doing.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order — trashing starts from doctrine's claim to coherence, not from the conclusion. The contradiction has to be located and shown to cut both ways before the legitimation claim follows.

parts.heading: Feminist legal theory: three starting points
parts.voice: structural — comparative, a reference students return to
body: Feminist legal theory is not one position but a family of positions that share a starting question — does law's claim to be objective and neutral survive scrutiny once you ask whose experience it was built around? — and disagree sharply about the answer and the remedy. Three broad strands recur in the literature, and distinguishing them precisely matters more than reciting any one of them well.

Liberal feminism takes law's existing categories — rights, equal treatment, non-discrimination — largely as sound, and argues the problem is under-inclusion: women were historically excluded from rights and opportunities that the liberal framework itself says should be universal, and the remedy is formal equality of treatment within that framework. Radical feminism, associated most closely with Catharine MacKinnon, argues this concedes too much: law is not a neutral arbiter that merely needs to be applied consistently to women, but an instrument that has helped construct and enforce male dominance, particularly over women's sexuality and bodies — so formal equal treatment, measured against a male-defined baseline, can reproduce the very inequality it claims to cure.

Difference feminism (drawing on work like Carol Gilligan's psychology of moral reasoning) takes a third route: it argues that women's moral and social experience is not simply excluded from law but genuinely different in kind — oriented more towards relationship, care and context than towards abstract rights and rules — and that law's rule-based, adversarial, rights-talk structure reflects a specifically male way of reasoning, marginalising an equally valid 'different voice' rather than a deficient one. Each strand answers the question 'what is wrong with the law' differently, and each faces a different set of objections — which is exactly why conflating them in an exam answer costs marks.

components.label: Three feminist starting points, compared
points: Liberal feminism — law's categories (rights, equal treatment) are basically sound; the problem is women's historical exclusion from them; remedy: formal equality within the existing framework

Radical feminism (MacKinnon) — law is not a neutral arbiter but an instrument that has helped construct male dominance, especially over sexuality; formal equal treatment measured against a male baseline can reproduce inequality rather than cure it

Difference feminism (drawing on Gilligan) — women's moral reasoning is authentically different, oriented to relationship and context rather than abstract rules; law's rule-based structure reflects a male way of reasoning and marginalises an equally valid alternative

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that liberal feminism seeks formal equality within law's existing categories, rather than arguing that those categories are themselves built on a male standpoint?
sliderLabels: Not confident — liberal feminism rejects the categories themselves
Confident — liberal feminism works within the existing categories
interaction.explanation: Confident is right. Liberal feminism's distinctive move is to treat rights and equal treatment as sound in principle and argue for women's fuller inclusion within them — it is radical feminism that argues the categories themselves encode a male standpoint.

parts.heading: MacKinnon: objectivity as the male point of view
parts.voice: text-first — reads MacKinnon's own words closely before generalising
body: Catharine MacKinnon's Toward a Feminist Theory of the State (1989) pushes the radical feminist argument to its sharpest form: not only does law fail to be neutral in particular doctrines, but the very idea of legal objectivity — of a view from nowhere, applied impartially — is itself a male standpoint mistaken for a universal one. MacKinnon's method connects legal theory to Marxism's method in a direct analogy: 'Sexuality is to feminism what work is to marxism: that which is most one's own, yet most taken away.' Where Marxism asks who controls the means of production, MacKinnon asks who controls the terms on which sexuality, and therefore much of women's social existence, is defined.

The clearest illustration in her own work is doctrinal: MacKinnon was centrally responsible for developing sexual harassment as a legally cognisable form of sex discrimination in US law, on the ground that treating it as a private, individual dispute (as tort or ordinary employment law tended to) obscured its systemic character as a mechanism of subordination. Her broader claim about rape law runs in parallel — that a legal standard built around what a 'reasonable man' would believe about consent measures the wrong's occurrence against the perspective of the person most likely to benefit from ambiguity, rather than from a genuinely neutral standpoint.

The conclusion MacKinnon draws is deliberately unsettling for legal method: if objectivity itself is the disputed terrain rather than a fixed point outside the dispute, then law cannot resolve the disagreement about women's subordination by 'applying the law neutrally' — because neutrality, on this account, is one of the things feminism has to argue about, not a shared premise both sides can retreat to.

components.citation: MacKinnon, Toward a Feminist Theory of the State (1989)
components.text: Sexuality is to feminism what work is to marxism: that which is most one's own, yet most taken away... Marxist theory argues that society is fundamentally constructed of the relations people form as they do and make things needed to survive humanly. Sexuality is that social process which creates, organizes, expresses, and directs desire, creating the social beings we know as women and men, as their relations create society.
elements: Draws a direct methodological analogy between sexuality (for feminism) and labour (for Marxism) as the object simultaneously constitutive of, and taken from, the subject
Treats sexuality as socially and legally constructed, not as a pre-political biological given that law simply regulates
Locates law as one of the sites where this construction happens, not a neutral space outside it

interaction.prompt: Which argument below is MacKinnon's dominance-approach argument, rather than a liberal-feminist equal-treatment argument?
interaction.scenarioA: A campaigner argues that a job qualification unrelated to genuine occupational need has historically excluded women, and calls for it to be applied identically to men and women so both compete under the same formal rule.
interaction.scenarioB: A campaigner argues that a legal test for consent, framed around what a 'reasonable person' would have believed, in practice measures ambiguity from a standpoint shaped by male experience, so 'equal application' of the test does not itself guarantee a fair outcome for women.
interaction.explanation: B is the dominance argument: the objection isn't unequal application of a sound standard, but that the standard's content already encodes a particular (male) point of view, so applying it 'equally' does not neutralise the problem. A is the liberal-feminist move — treat the existing category as sound and demand consistent application.

parts.heading: The critics' case against CLS and feminist legal theory
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the objections before assessing how much force they carry
body: Both traditions face serious, recurring academic objections, and stating them fairly is as much a skill this lesson tests as stating the original theories. Against CLS, three objections recur. First, the self-reference problem: if all legally-reasoned outcomes are indeterminate, produced by unstated political choice, on what basis is the CLS critique itself a determinate piece of legal-theoretical reasoning rather than just another political choice dressed up as analysis? Second, the empirical objection, pressed forcefully by writers sympathetic to law-and-economics and to Hart's own account: the vast majority of legal disputes are 'easy cases' that settle or resolve without genuine doctrinal contest at all — CLS's examples are disproportionately drawn from the hardest, most contested appellate cases, which may not be representative of law's ordinary operation. Third, the reconstructive gap: critics (including some sympathetic to the diagnosis) argue CLS was far stronger at 'trashing' doctrine than at building anything durable in its place, leaving practitioners with a critique they cannot act on.

Feminist legal theory faces objections both from outside and — importantly — from within feminist scholarship itself. The most significant internal challenge came from critical race feminists, notably Kimberlé Crenshaw and Angela Harris, who argued that MacKinnon's dominance approach, in generalising about 'women's' experience of subordination, implicitly universalised the experience of white, middle-class, heterosexual women and erased how race, class and sexuality change what subordination looks like and what would count as a remedy — an objection this module returns to directly in the next lesson. Difference feminism faces its own essentialism worry: critics ask whether an authentically 'different voice' is really a feature of womanhood as such, or a product of the same social roles feminism otherwise argues are contingent and changeable — in which case celebrating the difference risks entrenching the very roles that produced it.

None of this settles the debate, and it isn't meant to. What it should leave you with is a map: CLS's indeterminacy thesis and feminist legal theory's critique of neutrality are taken seriously by scholars precisely because they survive serious, repeated attack without collapsing outright — and because parts of each (sexual harassment law is the clearest doctrinal example) reshaped actual legal doctrine rather than staying academic.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often write that CLS and feminist legal theory are fringe or marginal positions that mainstream legal scholarship has simply dismissed.
components.whyItsWrong: Both traditions attract serious, ongoing academic engagement and criticism precisely because they are taken seriously, not because they are ignored — and radical feminist legal theory produced doctrinal change (sexual harassment as actionable sex discrimination is the clearest example) that most legal systems now treat as settled, whatever view is taken of the underlying theory.

interaction.prompt: Which of the following is the strongest version of the 'self-reference' objection to the CLS indeterminacy thesis?
options: CLS scholars have never held law faculty positions, so their critique lacks institutional standing
If all legally-reasoned outcomes are indeterminate and driven by unstated political choice, it is unclear why the CLS critique itself escapes that same charge
CLS scholars disagree with each other about tactics, which proves the theory is false
interaction.trapExplanation: The tempting wrong answers attack CLS's institutional position or internal disagreement, neither of which touches the theory's substance. The genuine philosophical difficulty is reflexive: a general claim that legal reasoning never compels outcomes has to explain why its own reasoning is an exception.

testPool.prompt: State the core claim of the CLS indeterminacy thesis.
acceptableAnswers: legal materials do not compel one determinate outcome
legal reasoning underdetermines results in contested cases
doctrine can be used to justify either side
testPool.modelAnswer: The accepted materials of legal reasoning — statute, precedent, interpretive canons — do not, by themselves, compel one determinate outcome in a significant range of contested cases; a further, non-legal (typically political or moral) choice supplies the missing premise.

testPool.prompt: In Kennedy's 'Form and Substance in Private Law Adjudication', 'individualism' and 'altruism' are best described as:
options: Two competing background value commitments coded into competing legal rules, neither dictated by legal reasoning itself
Two named legal doctrines with a clear rule of priority between them

testPool.prompt: Which of the following was NOT one of Unger's stated critiques of liberal legal thought in 'The Critical Legal Studies Movement'?
options: Formalism — treating legal reasoning as a distinct, quasi-mechanical method
Objectivism — treating doctrine as a coherent scheme of principle
The claim that judges should never give written reasons for a decision
The idea that doctrine legitimates a contingent settlement of social conflict as necessary
testPool.trapExplanation: CLS never argues judges should give no reasons — its claim is precisely that reasoned judgments can still be indeterminate. That option is an easy trap for students conflating 'indeterminate' with 'unreasoned'.

testPool.prompt: Order the steps of a Kennedy-style indeterminacy argument applied to a contract doctrine.
items: Identify the doctrine's rule-form (e.g. a fixed limitation period) and its standard-form alternative (e.g. a reasonableness test)
Show that each form serves a different background value — certainty/self-reliance versus context-sensitivity/mutual responsibility
Show a court could justify the same result, or its opposite, by foregrounding either value
Conclude the doctrine's 'correct' outcome depends on an unstated choice between individualism and altruism

testPool.prompt: Kennedy writes that legal rules can be arrayed on a spectrum from highly determinate ('rules') to highly general ('standards'). Which phrase from that framework best explains why a 'standard' like reasonableness increases a decision-maker's discretion compared with a fixed 'rule'?
options: A standard incorporates a background moral or policy judgment into its application, rather than settling that judgment in advance the way a fixed rule does
A standard is simply a rule with a longer statutory citation
A standard removes the judge's discretion entirely by requiring expert evidence

testPool.prompt: In the extract from MacKinnon below, highlight the sentence that most directly states her core methodological move.
testPool.passage: Sexuality is to feminism what work is to marxism: that which is most one's own, yet most taken away. Marxist theory argues that society is fundamentally constructed of the relations people form as they do and make things needed to survive humanly. Sexuality is that social process which creates, organizes, expresses, and directs desire, creating the social beings we know as women and men.
testPool.ratioSentence: Sexuality is to feminism what work is to marxism: that which is most one's own, yet most taken away.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that reflects an 'altruist' rather than an 'individualist' framing, in Kennedy's sense.
testPool.scenarioText: A buyer discovers a defect in goods a week after the statutory inspection window closed. A court applying the rule strictly would dismiss the claim outright. Instead, the court holds that because the seller could easily have flagged the defect and did not, the buyer's slightly late complaint should still be heard on its merits.
tappableSpans: the seller could easily have flagged the defect and did not
should still be heard on its merits
testPool.correctSpan: the seller could easily have flagged the defect and did not
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Right. Excusing strict compliance because the other party could easily have prevented the harm is the altruist move — it privileges mutual responsibility over the individualist value of holding parties strictly to agreed terms and deadlines.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the reasoning that shifts responsibility onto the other party's capacity to have prevented the problem — that relational, context-sensitive reasoning is what Kennedy labels altruist, as against a strict, rule-bound individualist reading.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario illustrates difference feminism's critique of law, rather than radical feminism's dominance critique?
testPool.scenarioA: A scholar argues a mediation-first family court model, favouring negotiated, relationship-preserving outcomes over adversarial rights assertions, better reflects a relational mode of moral reasoning than an adversarial model does.
testPool.scenarioB: A scholar argues that a legal definition of harm calibrated to physical injury systematically under-recognises the harms of coercive control, because the category of 'harm' was built around experiences more typical of men.
testPool.explanation: A is difference feminism: the objection is to law's adversarial, rule-based mode of reasoning itself, and the alternative offered is a relational one. B is the dominance-style argument: the objection is that a substantive legal category was built around a male-typical experience, which is closer to MacKinnon's critique of objectivity than to Gilligan-influenced difference feminism.

testPool.prompt: Two Court of Appeal panels, applying the same contractual 'good faith' standard to near-identical facts, reach opposite results — one enforcing a clause strictly, one excusing non-compliance. Which CLS concept best names what has happened?
options: The indeterminacy thesis — the standard's open texture allowed each panel to reach a different result while both remained faithful to the doctrine as stated
A simple error of law by one of the two panels, since only one reading can be correct
Neither panel actually applied the good faith standard at all
testPool.explanation: This is exactly the phenomenon CLS predicts: a standard (rather than a bright-line rule) leaves room for the background value choice — individualist or altruist — to determine the outcome, without either panel needing to depart from accepted doctrine to reach a different result.

testPool.prompt: A commercial court is asked to decide whether a supplier who missed a delivery deadline by two hours, after the buyer's own late payment caused the delay, is in breach. Using the CLS indeterminacy thesis, analyse why legal doctrine alone cannot dictate the answer.
factsToOrder: The contract specifies a fixed delivery deadline (a 'rule')
The buyer's own late payment contributed to the delay
A strict, individualist reading would hold the supplier to the deadline regardless of cause
An altruist reading would excuse the delay because the buyer's own conduct contributed to it

scaffolds.support: Full model answer shown, mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule given; student applies it to the facts and writes the conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full analysis unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the supplier is in breach, given the fixed deadline and the buyer's contribution to the delay.
modelAnswer.rule: Kennedy's indeterminacy thesis: private law doctrine oscillates between individualist readings (strict adherence to agreed terms) and altruist readings (excusing strict compliance where the other party's conduct contributed to the failure); neither reading is compelled by the doctrine itself.
modelAnswer.application: An individualist court holds the supplier to the deadline as agreed, treating the buyer's late payment as a separate issue to be litigated on its own terms. An altruist court treats the buyer's contribution to the delay as relevant to whether strict enforcement is fair, and excuses the breach. Both readings are available within the same doctrinal materials — the choice between them is not dictated by the contract's wording alone.
modelAnswer.conclusion: There is no single doctrinally-compelled answer; which result is 'correct' depends on an unstated choice between individualist and altruist background values, which is the indeterminacy thesis's point.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that CLS scholars claim every legal question, including routine and uncontested ones, is equally indeterminate?
sliderLabels: Not confident — CLS targets contested, hard cases, not all legal questions
Confident — CLS claims all legal questions are equally indeterminate
testPool.correctPosition: CLS targets contested, hard cases, not all legal questions
testPool.explanation: Not confident is the defensible position, and it is also where CLS's critics press hardest: the empirical objection is precisely that CLS's examples are disproportionately drawn from hard, contested appellate cases, which may not represent how most legal questions are actually resolved.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that best supports a MacKinnon-style dominance critique of this scenario, rather than a liberal-feminist equal-treatment critique.
testPool.scenarioText: A workplace tribunal applies a 'reasonable person' standard to decide whether a supervisor's repeated comments about a colleague's appearance amounted to harassment. The tribunal concludes a reasonable person would not have found the comments threatening, because they were framed as compliments.
tappableSpans: A workplace tribunal applies a 'reasonable person' standard
repeated comments about a colleague's appearance
a reasonable person would not have found the comments threatening
testPool.correctSpan: a reasonable person would not have found the comments threatening
testPool.explanation: The dominance critique targets the content of the standard itself — whose experience 'reasonable' encodes — rather than whether the standard was applied consistently. The finding that a 'reasonable person' would not find repeated appearance-focused comments threatening is exactly the kind of outcome MacKinnon argues reveals a male-calibrated baseline.

testPool.prompt: A family court, choosing between two custody models, favours one that prioritises ongoing negotiated contact over a strict, rights-based allocation of time. A scholar praises this as reflecting an authentically relational mode of reasoning. Which strand of feminist legal theory does this praise best exemplify — and what is the strongest objection a critic could raise?
options: Difference feminism; the objection is that celebrating a 'relational' mode risks entrenching the social roles that produced it rather than showing it is an inherent feature of womanhood
Liberal feminism; the objection is that mediation models are procedurally more expensive than adversarial ones
Radical feminism; the objection is that mediation models were invented by men
testPool.explanation: This is difference feminism's characteristic move — praising a relational, context-sensitive alternative to rights-based adjudication — and its most serious academic objection is the essentialism worry: is the 'different voice' really constitutive of womanhood, or a product of contingent social roles feminism elsewhere argues should change?

testPool.prompt: In the extract from Unger below, highlight the sentence that most directly states law's legitimating function.
testPool.passage: Legal doctrine takes the existing, historically contingent settlement of social conflict and re-describes it as the natural, principled working-out of impersonal legal categories. That re-description is what legitimates the settlement: it makes an outcome that could have gone otherwise look as though it had to come out this way.
testPool.ratioSentence: That re-description is what legitimates the settlement: it makes an outcome that could have gone otherwise look as though it had to come out this way.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is collapsing distinct positions into one another — treating CLS's indeterminacy thesis and MacKinnon's dominance critique as the same argument, or conflating liberal, radical and difference feminism. Each has a distinct claim, a distinct target, and a distinct objection; the test items are built to reward keeping them separate.
